title: Iterators, Invalidation and the Algorithm Library
objectives: Match standard algorithms to the iterator categories they require and explain why some containers reject std::sort
Remove elements from a vector safely with the erase-remove idiom and explain why std::remove alone is not enough
Use std::sort, std::lower_bound, std::upper_bound and std::accumulate on price data with correct semantics
Identify iterator invalidation when mutating during iteration and write the safe loop patterns
motivation: Algorithms are where C++ pays for its strictness: std::sort on a million prices finishes while a hand-written loop is still warming up, and std::lower_bound finds a price level in 20 comparisons instead of a million. But every algorithm speaks the language of iterators, and iterators die when containers mutate underneath them. This lesson covers the categories, the invalidation traps, and the handful of algorithms a quant developer uses daily.

blocks.md: Every STL algorithm operates on a half-open range [first, last) described by two iterators. The iterator's **category** declares what it can do: input iterators read forward once; forward iterators can re-read and make multiple passes; bidirectional iterators also step back; random-access iterators jump to any offset in O(1), like pointers. std::vector, std::array and std::deque deliver random-access iterators; std::list, std::map and std::set are bidirectional; the unordered containers are forward-only. Algorithms state the minimum category they require, and the compiler enforces it at build time.

blocks.md: The enforcement matters because std::sort needs random access to swap distant elements efficiently; calling it on a list's iterators simply does not compile, and list::sort exists precisely because it can relink nodes instead of moving elements. When you need a sorted view of a hash table, copy the pairs into a vector and sort there: the copy is $O(n)$ and the sort $O(n \log n)$ - and the copy into contiguous memory is usually faster than it looks.

blocks.caption: Partitioning in action: each level of quicksort touches all n elements and there are about log n levels. O(n log n) made visible.

blocks.md: A range-for grabs begin() and end() once, then walks. If the body erases from or pushes into the same vector, the cached end() and the current iterator can dangle: undefined behaviour, often invisible in debug builds and a crash in release. The fix is to own the loop and use the return value of erase, which hands back the next valid iterator.

blocks.caption: Prints 1 3 5 (trailing space and all), the loop survives because erase re-seats the iterator.

blocks.md: Filtering out many values has a better shape than one-at-a-time. std::remove(first, last, value) shifts the kept elements forward and returns an iterator to the new logical end, but it cannot erase anything, because it holds no container. The tail elements are left in an unspecified state and size() is unchanged. Erasing is the container's job: v.erase(newEnd, v.end()) truncates. Together the two calls are the **erase-remove idiom**.

blocks.caption: remove shifts survivors forward; erase truncates the stale tail.

blocks.title: std::remove does not remove
blocks.md: std::remove moves survivors forward and returns a past-the-end iterator for the kept range; it never calls erase and never shrinks size(). After remove alone, the vector's tail holds stale copies and size() is still the old value. C++20 adds std::erase_if(v, pred), which fuses both steps, but C++17 code lives on the idiom.

blocks.text: Sorting and binary search on prices

blocks.caption: Output: 1, 3, true, the two bounds bracket the whole run of 100.50s.

blocks.md: lower_bound returns the first position whose element is not less than the target; upper_bound the first strictly greater. On the sorted ladder 99.75, 100.50, 100.50, 101.00 the two bounds are positions 1 and 3, and that half-open range is exactly the set of resting orders at price 100.50. Both are $O(\log n)$ on random-access iterators, but they require the range to be sorted ascending under the same comparator; on unsorted data they return garbage, not an error.

std::accumulate(first, last, init) folds the range into init with +. The initializer's type matters more than people expect: the accumulator is a copy of init, so accumulate over a vector<double> with init 0 sums in **integer** arithmetic and truncates every step. Pass 0.0 for a floating-point fold. And because floating-point addition is not associative, the sum of a return series depends on its order, a fact that matters at book scale.

blocks.caption: The accumulator's type is the init's type, 0 means integer arithmetic throughout.

blocks.title: Sums have an order
blocks.md: Floating-point addition is not associative: (0.1 + 0.2) + 0.3 differs from 0.1 + (0.2 + 0.3) in the last bits. Over millions of returns the drift is real, so numerical desks use pairwise or Kahan summation (std::accumulate cannot; C++17's std::reduce with execution policies may reassociate deliberately). Know your accumulator's precision budget before quoting a PnL to eight decimals.

params.title: Finding a target price in a sorted vector of n prices

blocks.caption: Sorting once costs O(n log n) and buys O(log n) searches forever after, 20 comparisons instead of a million.

guidedExercise.prompt: Given std::vector<int> v{5, 9, 2, 9, 7, 9}: (a) after v.erase(std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 9), v.end()), state size() and the contents. (b) After std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()), state the contents and the indices returned by std::lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), 5) and std::upper_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), 5). (c) State std::accumulate over the sorted vector with initial value 0.
hints: remove shifts survivors forward; erase truncates the tail.
lower_bound is the first index whose element is >= the target.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) The survivors 5, 2, 7 shift forward, so size() = **3** and contents are {5, 2, 7}. (b) Sorted: {2, 5, 7}; lower_bound(5) = index **1** (first element >= 5), upper_bound(5) = index **2** (first element > 5). (c) $2 + 5 + 7 = $ **14**.

independentExercise.prompt: A replay log is std::vector<int> ticks{11, 12, 12, 13, 11, 14}. Using STL algorithms only: (a) count the 11s; (b) erase all 12s with the erase-remove idiom and give size() and the contents; (c) sort the vector and report the values at *std::min_element and *std::max_element; (d) compute the total with std::accumulate and the mean as a double (total divided by size in double arithmetic).
hints: std::count(first, last, value) returns the number of occurrences.
The mean needs a double division: static_cast<double>(total) / ticks.size().

commonMistakes: Erasing inside a range-for loop, begin() and end() are cached once and dangle after the first erase; use it = v.erase(it) or erase-remove.
Calling std::remove and expecting the vector to shrink, remove only shifts survivors; the erase call does the truncating.
Calling std::lower_bound on an unsorted range, the result is meaningless garbage, not an error.
Accumulating doubles with an integer init of 0, every partial sum is truncated; pass 0.0.
Trying std::sort on a std::list, its iterators are only bidirectional; use the member sort or copy to a vector.
realWorldApplication: Tick-data filtering, sorted ladders, session-level aggregations and binary-search lookups into history are all loops over the algorithms in this lesson; the invalidation rules decide whether the surrounding code survives refactoring.
quantFinanceApplication: Sorting a day's prints and slicing the equal-range at a price is exactly how resting-volume-at-price queries are served; accumulate-style folds over return vectors are the innermost loop of every backtest and risk report.
summary: Iterator categories run input -> forward -> bidirectional -> random access; vector/array/deque are random access, list/map/set bidirectional, unordered_* forward.
std::sort requires random-access iterators and is O(n log n); std::lower_bound needs at least forward iterators and is O(log n) only on random access.
The erase-remove idiom (std::remove + v.erase) filters a vector in O(n); remove alone shifts survivors and never shrinks size().
lower_bound is the first element >= target, upper_bound the first strictly greater, together they bracket the equal range.
std::accumulate folds with the init's type as the accumulator: integer init truncates; float sums depend on order.

quiz.prompt: Which iterator category does std::sort require?
quiz.explanation: Quicksort-style partitioning swaps distant elements and needs O(1) jumps, random access. That is why list has its own member sort, which relinks nodes instead.
std::remove shifts the survivors 5, 2, 7 forward and returns the new logical end, size() is untouched at 6. Only the erase call truncates the stale tail, leaving size 3.

Sorting gives 99.75, 100.50, 100.50, 101.00. lower_bound(100.50) is the first element >= 100.50 at index 1; upper_bound is the first strictly greater at index 3; binary_search finds 101.00, so boolalpha prints true.

quiz.prompt: With std::vector<int> v{5, 9, 2, 9, 7, 9}; after v.erase(std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 9), v.end()); what is v.size()?
quiz.explanation: Three nines are removed: the survivors 5, 2, 7 are shifted forward and the tail of three elements is erased, leaving size 3.

quiz.prompt: Which of these compile and are correct when handed std::list<int>::iterators?
options: std::lower_bound (given the list is kept sorted)
quiz.explanation: List iterators are bidirectional: find needs input, accumulate needs input, and lower_bound needs only forward, all satisfied (lower_bound degrades to O(n) without random access). std::sort requires random access and does not compile; use the member list::sort, O(n log n) via node relinking.

quiz.prompt: Why is erasing from a std::vector inside a range-for loop undefined behaviour?
quiz.modelAnswer: The range-for caches begin() and end() once; erase invalidates the current iterator and shifts elements past the cached end, so the loop walks dangling iterators.
quiz.explanation: The loop holds two iterators it never updates; the first erase invalidates them (or the elements they designate). The manual pattern works because erase's return value re-seats the iterator after every mutation.

flashcards.front: Name the STL iterator categories, weakest to strongest.
flashcards.back: Input (single-pass read) -> Output (single-pass write) -> Forward (multi-pass) -> Bidirectional (also steps back) -> Random access (O(1) jumps, pointer-like). vector/array/deque: random access; list/map/set: bidirectional; unordered_*: forward.

flashcards.front: vector<int> v{5,9,2,9,7,9}; v.erase(std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 9), v.end()); cout << v.size();
flashcards.back: 3, remove shifted the survivors {5, 2, 7} forward and returned the new logical end; erase truncated the stale tail.

flashcards.front: lower_bound vs upper_bound on a sorted range
flashcards.back: lower_bound: first element >= target. upper_bound: first element > target. Together they bracket the run of elements equal to the target; both O(log n) on random-access iterators, and the range must be sorted ascending.
sort: O(n log n) comparisons, random-access required. lower_bound/upper_bound: O(log n) on random access, O(n) on forward-only. accumulate: O(n) with the init's type as the accumulator type.
